alternates: Why Developers Misjudge How Much AI Speeds Them Up
The Study Where Developers Felt 20% Faster and Were 19% Slower
stories.question: Do developers know whether AI is actually making them faster?
stories.whyWatch: Every developer has a feeling about this. Two randomized trials checked the feeling against the stopwatch and got opposite answers, which is the most useful thing a viewer can learn about their own estimate.
stories.tension: METR: developers forecast 24% faster, felt 20% faster, were 19% slower. Peng's Copilot trial: both groups guessed about 35% and the measured gain was 55.8%. Overestimate in one, underestimate in the other.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Trials that record developers' predicted or perceived speedup alongside a measured one, on comparable tasks.
gaps: What explains the split between METR 2025 RCT, Copilot RCT (Peng), METR 2026 update?

METR 2026 update: METR Feb 2026: some developers self-report very high speedups, which METR notes can be 'quite unreliable' per its earlier study; it also says the true speedup may be higher among those who selected out, so no new measured overestimate.
stories.premise: The disagreement is the story and it is well measured on both sides. METR 2025 (16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks in their own mature repos, early-2025 tools) found a 19% slowdown against a forecast of 24% faster and an after-the-fact estimate of 20% faster; experts predicted 38-39%. Peng's 2023 Copilot trial (freelancers, a greenfield HTTP server task) found a 55.8% speedup that participants underestimated at about 35%. METR's 2026 update adds that self-reports can be very unreliable and that its new data are too selection-biased to measure. The likely explanation, task familiarity and codebase maturity, is the resolution the video should offer as a hypothesis, not a finding.

arc.hook: Ask the viewer to guess how much faster AI makes them, then show what happened when two trials asked the same of their participants.
arc.conflict: Two randomized trials, opposite errors: experienced maintainers overestimated and got slower; freelancers on a fresh task underestimated and got much faster.
arc.evidence: METR's forecast-versus-measured numbers and acceptance rates; Peng's estimate-versus-measured numbers; METR 2026's warning about self-reports and selection.
arc.resolution: Perception tracks effort saved on the parts AI does, not time spent on the parts it creates; which dominates depends on task familiarity and codebase maturity (a hypothesis both papers gesture at).
arc.takeaway: Measure, don't ask: time a week of comparable tasks with and without the tool.

coherence.explanation: One question: can developers tell whether AI is speeding them up? Two trials measured perception against the clock and disagree.

stories.title: How Much Faster Does AI Actually Make Programmers?
alternates: 2x, 10x, or Slower? What the Trials Found
The METR Study Everyone Cites, Explained
stories.question: How much faster does AI actually make programmers?
stories.whyWatch: The claims run from 10x to 'it slows you down', and both extremes cite studies. The trials fit together once you look at who was measured doing what.
stories.tension: Ten-times claims against field trials in the twenties of percent and one trial that found experienced maintainers 19% slower.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Randomized or quasi-experimental measurements of task time or output with and without AI tools, on real work, by setting.
evidenceAvailable: Shan et al. field study + RCT: partly (0.5, partial)
Shan et al. field study + RCT: wrong (0.3, partial)
gaps: Google migrations report is context only: bespoke migration pipelines with fine-tuned models and engineers' estimates; not average developer work in an enterprise codebase
No study strong enough to decide: "Engineers who adopt agentic coding are about ten times as productive as peers who don't"
stories.premise: Field trials put the average gain in the twenties: Microsoft/Accenture (4,867 developers, 26% more weekly PRs), Google (96 engineers, about 21% less time on an enterprise task, confidence interval crossing zero) and Shan's field study (18% more user stories, self-selected usage). METR 2025 found the opposite sign for 16 experienced open-source maintainers in their own mature repos: 19% slower with early-2025 tools. The 10x claim has no supporting measurement; the field gain and Anthropic's self-reported 50% bound it, and neither measured agentic coding. METR's 2026 update says the slowdown was probably specific to early 2025 but calls its new data very weak evidence because of selection effects. Google's migration figures (50% to 89% savings) are bespoke pipelines and engineers' estimates, context only.

arc.hook: Three numbers on screen: 10x, 26%, minus 19%. All of them come with a study attached.
arc.conflict: The hype and the slowdown both cite trials; the question is what each trial measured.
arc.evidence: Microsoft/Accenture, Google and Shan on real work; METR 2025 on mature repos with experts; METR 2026 on what changed and why it cannot tell; the absence of any 10x measurement.
arc.resolution: Twenties of percent on average work, less or negative for experts in familiar code, unknown for today's agentic tools; 10x is unmeasured.
arc.takeaway: Expect a quarter, not a multiple, and expect less on the code you know best.

coherence.explanation: One question, the size of the productivity gain, answered by the field trials' estimate, the slowdown trial, the 10x claim it bounds, and the argument that newer models change the answer. The perception claim is its own story and is dropped.

stories.title: Does AI Help Junior or Senior Developers More?
alternates: Who Really Gets the AI Productivity Boost?
The Experience Paradox in AI Coding Studies
stories.question: Does AI help junior or senior developers more?
stories.whyWatch: Influencers say AI is a multiplier for experts. Most trials found the opposite, one found a hint the other way, and the reason they differ says something about when the tools help anyone.
stories.tension: 'Amplifies experts far more' against trials where juniors and short-tenure developers gained most and experienced maintainers were slowed.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Trials that split the measured gain by experience or codebase familiarity, on the same tasks.
evidenceAvailable: Shan et al. field study + RCT: wrong (0.45, direct)
Shan et al. field study + RCT: partly (0.35, direct)
Echoes of AI maintainability RCT: right (0.5, partial)

stories.premise: The 'far more for experts' claim is not supported: Microsoft's field experiment (short-tenure 27-39% versus long-tenure 8-13%, mostly not significant), Shan's RCT, Peng's Copilot trial and the code-ownership experiment all found gains concentrated among less experienced developers, and METR found experienced maintainers slowed, more so on tasks they knew well. The Google trial is the exception: on code unfamiliar to everyone, seniors gained if anything more, not significantly. That pattern is the resolution: gains concentrate where the developer lacks context, which juniors usually do and seniors do on unfamiliar code. Skill in using the tools matters (habitual AI users' code scored better downstream in the Echoes trial) but the evidence for a steep skill curve is thin and partly self-reported, and METR saw no improvement over the first 50 hours.

arc.hook: Two engineers, one senior, one junior, both switch on the same tool. The influencers say the senior pulls ahead. The trials say otherwise.
arc.conflict: Five trials point one way, Google's points the other, and 'far more' for experts has no support anywhere.
arc.evidence: Microsoft/Accenture by tenure, Shan's moderation analysis, Peng's heterogeneity, the code-ownership experiment, METR's slowdown by task familiarity, and Google's unfamiliar-code design.
arc.resolution: The tools help most where the developer has the least context. Juniors have less of it everywhere; seniors have less of it on unfamiliar code. Using the tools well is a skill, but not yet a measured steep one.
arc.takeaway: Point the tools at unfamiliar work, expect less on code you know by heart, and treat '10x for experts' as marketing.

coherence.explanation: One question, who gains more from AI coding tools, answered by the senior-versus-junior results across six trials, the concentration of gains on unfamiliar or routine work, and the role of skill in using the tools.

arc.resolution: No measured maintainability penalty yet, within the limits of one small trial; a measured understanding penalty for the author; and issue counts that need a baseline before they mean 'more'.

The Cleanup Cost Nobody Has Measured Well
stories.question: Does AI-generated code follow your codebase's conventions?
stories.whyWatch: Every team that adopts the tools reports the cleanup, and the few numbers behind that complaint are weaker than they sound.
stories.tension: Every source points the same way, and none measures it well.
stories.evidenceNeeded: A measured rate of convention violations in AI commits against a human baseline, from an independent study of real repositories.

LLM coding-style study (FSE 2025): On CoderEval's repository-context Python tasks, 66.2% to 90.1% of functionally correct samples from five models (CodeLlama, StarCoder2, two DeepSeekCoder sizes, GPT-4) differ in coding style from the project's own human-written solution; a measured rate against real repository code, but the repositories had no specific style requirements and style difference from one reference solution is not the same as violating an established convention.

Claude Code PRs study (TOSEM): Of 214 merged Claude Code PRs (out of 475 merged, 567 total, 157 projects) that were modified before merge, 50 (23.4%) got style revisions such as enforcing naming conventions, fixing formatting and resolving linter warnings the agent missed, which the authors read as agents underperforming on project-specific style rules; a measured rate, but only about one merged PR in ten, and no style breakdown is given for the human PR baseline.

Debt study (302k AI commits): Correctness issues dominated by undefined variables (23,856) lead authors to say AI code 'may look locally correct, but still fail to stay consistent with the surrounding context'; this is consistency with surrounding code, not style conventions specifically.

Vibe-coding literature review: WL27 is quoted saying conversationally generated code 'often lacks cohesive structure, consistent patterns, and proper documentation'; this is a single peer-reviewed source, not a measured drift rate.
stories.premise: Every source leans the same way: AI-generated code fits a codebase's conventions less well than the code around it. But each measures something narrower. The only comparison with human pull requests is a vendor's: CodeRabbit, which sells AI code review, scored 470 open-source pull requests with its own issue taxonomy and found formatting problems and naming inconsistencies roughly two to three times as common in those it flagged as AI-co-authored, while saying it cannot guarantee the others were human-only. stories.title: Do Vibe-Coded Apps Survive Production?
alternates: Prototype in a Day, Rewrite in a Month?
Where the Evidence on Vibe Coding Runs Out
stories.question: Do vibe-coded apps survive contact with production?
stories.whyWatch: Sixteen sources say vibe-coded apps break in production. A review says the prototype half is well supported; an audit of 200 live vibe-coded apps shows what breaking looks like, and what nobody has measured yet.
stories.tension: The literature review finds almost no production evidence; the first audit of deployed vibe-coded apps finds 91% of them with at least one security flaw. The belief is half shown on security and unmeasured on everything else.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Case series or longitudinal data on vibe-coded apps taken to production, with a human-built comparison group, on security, reliability, scaling and maintenance.
evidenceAvailable: Vibe-coded apps security audit (200 deployed): partly (0.5, partial)
gaps: Reviewer: Strongest study 0.36 after applicability. The review supports only the prototype half; the security audit of 200 deployed vibe-coded apps (91% with a validated vulnerability) shows one kind of production failure but measures neither functional breakdown nor scaling and has no human-built baseline. Unblocked by a study comparing vibe-coded with conventionally built apps in production (incidents, outages, rewrites or vulnerabilities per app), or following vibe-coded apps over time as they gain users.
stories.premise: Before checking, the best guess was "right". Two documents bear on it, each on one half. The 47-source multivocal review (2022 to October 2025) finds evidence strongest for prototyping and UI work and weakest for production, data-intensive and safety-critical use: the prototype half is supported, the production half mostly unstudied. The security audit (Deng, Fan, Meng 2026) took 200 randomly sampled publicly deployed open-source apps that were at least 90% AI-authored with Claude Code or Lovable and found at least one manually validated vulnerability in 91% of them, 65.8% of the 1,186 rated Critical or High, mostly broken access control, injection and authentication; one failure mode it names is demo-oriented design (static demo keys, placeholder auth). Limits the video must carry: the audit measures security only, not whether the apps stop working or fail to scale; it has no human-built comparison group, and ordinary web apps also often carry flaws; it covers GitHub apps from two agents; and no study follows vibe-coded apps over time in production.

arc.resolution: On security, deployed vibe-coded apps do commonly break, in the sense of shipping exploitable flaws to real users. arc.takeaway: Treat a vibe-coded app as a prototype until someone has checked its access control, inputs and authentication; the claim that it breaks at scale is still an expectation, not a finding.

stories.question: Can you ignore the generated code if the specification is good enough?
stories.whyWatch: Eight sources say spec-to-code without reading the output fails, two say it works; the corpus has the understanding-loss experiment and little else.
stories.tension: A workflow argument with one adjacent experiment.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Outcomes of teams that ship generated code unread versus teams that review it, on defects and later change cost.
evidenceAvailable: Post-merge fate study (182 repos): partly (0.45, partial)
gaps: Reviewer: The post-merge fate study links merging agentic code without review to more later corrective maintenance, but only as a project-level association (R2 6%) with no measure of spec quality; the code-ownership experiment shows understanding loss and the vibe-coding review only recommends reading code. Unblocking needs a comparison of spec-driven teams that ship generated code unread against teams that review it, on defects, incidents or later change cost, holding spec quality fixed.
What explains the split between Post-merge fate study (182 repos), Vibe-coding literature review, Code-ownership experiment (Martin-Lopez)?

Post-merge fate study (182 repos): Across 177 open-source projects, the share of merged pull requests that got no code review was the strongest predictor of how much more corrective maintenance agentic code needed than human code (about 6% more burden per 10 percentage points of no-review rate, HR multiplier 1.75, CI 1.01-3.04); an observational, project-level association with a weak overall fit (R2 6%), and it measures merging without review, not a spec-driven workflow that ignores the code.

Vibe-coding literature review: The review recommends reviewing generated code before committing rather than integrating unread output, and warns that deferred understanding (cognitive debt) raises later maintenance costs; this is recommendation-level evidence.

Code-ownership experiment (Martin-Lopez): The authors warn that a loss of understanding may hurt review, debugging and maintenance. They also concede that future workflows handing those jobs to agents might make low-level comprehension matter less. So the paper backs the concern only speculatively.

stories.title: Can You Leave an AI Agent Running on Your Backlog?
alternates: What Happens When Agents Open Their Own Pull Requests
Unattended Agents: What Gets Merged
stories.question: Can you leave an AI agent running on your backlog unattended?
stories.whyWatch: Six sources sell the loop; across hundreds of thousands of agent pull requests in the wild, between a third and two thirds were merged, every one after a human looked at it.
stories.tension: The promise of an agent clearing a backlog alone against merge rates well below human contributors'.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Outcomes of agents left to work on real backlogs: share merged without rework, human review time per merged change, regressions introduced.
gaps: Reviewer: Strongest study 0.27 after applicability. AIDev (456K agent pull requests) gives only merge rates for autonomous agents (Codex 64%, Devin 49%, Copilot 35%, all below humans), not goal or loop commands and with no rework or regression measure; Airbnb is one bespoke migration pipeline. Needs a controlled or longitudinal study of agents left on real backlogs measuring share merged without rework, human review time per merged change and regressions after merge.
What explains the split between AIDev agent PRs (456K), Airbnb migration?

AIDev agent PRs (456K): In AIDev's PRs from popular repositories (over 500 stars), autonomous agents that take a task and open a pull request on their own had 35% (GitHub Copilot), 49% (Devin) and 64% (OpenAI Codex) of their PRs merged, 15 to 40 points below human PRs and lowest on features, bug fixes and performance; the agents do produce work without step-by-step prompting, but every change still went through human review and a third to two thirds were not merged.

Airbnb migration: Airbnb's custom loop runner re-prompted the LLM with errors until a step passed or a retry cap was hit, and the first bulk run migrated 75% of 3.5K files in 4 hours; this is a bespoke pipeline, not a generic agent goal command.
stories.premise: Sources say goal or loop commands let an agent work through a backlog unattended. The evidence says partly. Airbnb's bespoke retry pipeline, with a retry cap, migrated 75% of 3.5K test files on its first bulk run, one migration and not a generic command. In AIDev's pull requests from popular open-source repositories, autonomous agents had 35% (GitHub Copilot), 49% (Devin) and 64% (OpenAI Codex) of their pull requests merged, 15 to 40 points below human contributors and lowest on features and bug fixes; every merge passed human review, and neither source measures rework before merging or regressions after.

arc.hook: Several sources say you can hand an agent a goal, let it loop, and come back to a cleared backlog.
arc.conflict: The one documented loop is a custom pipeline built for one migration, and the large count of agent pull requests in the wild shows far fewer merged than the promise implies.
arc.evidence: Airbnb's retry pipeline (75% of 3.5K files on the first run, with a retry cap) beside AIDev's merge rates for Codex, Devin and Copilot against human pull requests in the same repositories.
arc.resolution: Agents do produce work without step-by-step prompting, but on general code a third to two thirds of it is merged, each piece after human review; the narrow, checkable migration went further. Rework and regressions are not measured.
arc.takeaway: An agent can work a backlog in the background; it cannot be left unattended, because a person still decides what merges.
